newsitem.title: SWEDEN: CURRENCY EFFECTS BOOST VOLVO FIRST HALF PROFITS.
newsitem.headline: CURRENCY EFFECTS BOOST VOLVO FIRST HALF PROFITS.

text.p: Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo said on Tuesday currency effects helped boost its first half profits by about one billion crowns and that its truck division was still making a loss in North America.

The company posted an operating profit of 3.95 billion crowns in the first six months of the year compared to 2.28 billion in the same 1996 period. Net sales rose to 89.02 billion crowns from 78.06 billion.
Profit after financial items rose to 7.95 billion crowns from 3.86 billion, including capital gains.

Volvo said earlier the first half profit would include a one-off gain of 3.03 billion crowns from the sale of its Pripps Ringnes stake and of 221 million crowns from the sale of a stake in the airline SAS.
"Positive currency effects totalled one billion crowns, taking futures and options contracts into account," Volvo said in its results statement.

"The increase was attributable to larger volumes of sales, higher margins and the favourable effects of foreign exchange movements; this gain was offset in part by higher costs for research and development, and for marketing," Volvo said.

Improved sales in all sectors, except Volvo Trucks, fuelled the 14 percent increase in sales, Volvo said. Operating profit for its car division rose to 2.15 billion crowns from 187 million a year earlier. In the short term Volvo said it had

to restore Volvo Trucks' North American operations, which slipped into the red in the second quarter of this year. Volvo Truck posted a global operating profit of 688 million crowns compared to 1.08 billion.
"Major rationalisation and cost-saving programmes have been instituted but have not yet had full effect, Aggressive improvements must continue," it said.
It said the Volvo VN, a truck based on the FH concept especially for the North American market, had been well-received.
The operating margin for the cars division increased to 4.5 percent from 0.5 percent.
Volvo said the total market for passenger cars declined slightly during the first half of the year.
"The North American market decreased by approximately four percent while the market in Europe was approximately at the 1996 level," it said.
The Japanese market increase by five percent but this was mainly in the first quarter. A tax increase in Japan in hurt sales in the second quarter.
The number of cars sold rose 12 percent to 196,200 and the car division's net sales climbed 21 percent to 48.16 billion crowns.
The favourable sales trend in Europe from the beginning of the year continued in the second quarter.
